title: Who gets to decide what AI can do?
description: Companies write the first rules. Public institutions and the people affected need meaningful ways to shape and challenge what happens next.
body:
Imagine a school considering an AI tutor. Teachers want students to get useful explanations. Parents want their children's information protected. Students want help without being watched constantly. The company supplying the system has its own rules about what the tutor may discuss.

Who gets the final say?

That hypothetical classroom captures a question running through the AI debate: who should decide what these systems are allowed to do, especially when their decisions affect people who never chose to use them?

There is no single decision to hand over. Building an AI model, selling access to it, putting it into a school and deciding how a student can challenge its advice are different responsibilities. A sensible approach needs room for technical expertise, public rules and the people living with the consequences.

## The first rules come from the people building it

An AI company's choices shape what users can do. A concrete example arrived on October 8, when Anthropic announced changes to Claude's usage policy, scheduled to take effect November 12. It clarified restrictions involving surveillance, weapons and autonomous physical actions. It also removed a blanket prohibition on personalized political targeting, while retaining restrictions on deception and misuse of personal data. [Read the policy announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update)

The change illustrates a real judgment call. A broad restriction can block harmful activity and legitimate work at the same time. Anthropic cited multilingual voter information and ballot-correction notices as examples of civic work caught by the earlier rule.

That does not establish that the revised approach will prevent abuse. It shows why setting boundaries requires choices about whose activities to permit, what evidence to demand and which risks to accept.

Developers have valuable technical knowledge. They also have commercial interests. Both matter when assessing a company's proposal for how everyone else should be governed.

## A promise, a policy and a law have different force

On October 18, Anthropic proposed committing 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, subject to stockholder approval. Its announcement described a wholly owned entity and said more governance details would follow. [Read the announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/public-benefit-fund)

That could support worthwhile work. But allocating money to public benefit does not, by itself, give the public authority over how AI is developed or deployed. The questions are different: who receives the benefits, and who makes the decisions?

Voluntary standards can help organisations make those decisions more carefully. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework offers guidance for managing risks across design, development, use and evaluation. NIST explicitly describes it as voluntary. Following a framework and being legally required to meet a standard are different arrangements. [Read NIST's overview](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

In the European Union, the AI Act takes a legal, risk-based approach. The European Commission describes responsibilities for both developers and organisations using AI, with enforcement shared between the AI Office and national authorities. Its implementation is phased; readers should not assume every obligation is already in effect. [Read the Commission's current overview](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai)

Law can establish public boundaries and consequences that a company cannot simply rewrite in its terms of service. Whether those boundaries work still depends on their design, enforcement and opportunities to challenge misuse of power. Government authority deserves scrutiny too: rules can become politically selective, and expensive compliance can disadvantage smaller organisations. Those are reasons to demand transparent, proportionate oversight and independent review of the overseers.

## The school still has a decision to make

Return to our imaginary tutor. Even a legally sold product with a published safety policy leaves the school with practical choices. Will it merely suggest explanations, or help grade students? What information will it receive? Can a teacher override it? Can a family ask for a different arrangement?

Those are proposed questions for the school, not claims that every jurisdiction already guarantees those rights.

The same distinction applies to a hospital or employer. A supplier's general assurances cannot answer whether a particular use is appropriate for particular people. A person assigned to supervise a system also needs the time, information and authority to intervene. A human name on an approval form offers little reassurance if disagreement has no effect.

## Would opening the technology spread the power?

One response is to let more people inspect and adapt AI themselves. With an open-weight model, the numerical parameters learned during training are available to download. That is more access than a chatbot interface provides, though it does not necessarily include the training data or everything needed to reproduce the model. [The Columbia report discusses these degrees of openness](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.22183).

A 2025 report from a convening of researchers, engineers and policy specialists argues that openness can support independent scrutiny, local safeguards and a wider range of perspectives. It also identifies shortcomings in testing across languages and in protecting AI agents from attacks. These are workshop findings and recommendations, not proof that open models are always safer. [Read the report's summary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22183)

Sharing access can distribute useful capabilities. It can also make harmful modifications harder for the original developer to control. Access alone does not supply the expertise, computing resources or institutional influence needed to participate equally.

The practical question is which forms of access allow useful scrutiny and legitimate work, and which safeguards remain effective once that access is granted.

## Public input can go beyond a feedback box

There are small, concrete experiments to learn from. In 2023, Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project asked roughly 1,000 Americans to propose and vote on principles for an AI assistant. Researchers used that input to train an experimental model. [Read the experiment](https://www.anthropic.com/research/collective-constitutional-ai-aligning-a-language-model-with-public-input)

The limits are instructive. The sample was American and screened for familiarity with AI. Researchers still chose how to moderate suggestions, combine statements and translate them into training principles. This was an experiment in participation, not a public election controlling a deployed service.

Still, it demonstrated a way for people outside a lab to contribute to model design. Future efforts could give affected communities a clearer role, publish how their input changed a decision and explain which decisions remain outside their control.

## A useful test: can anyone challenge the decision?

My standard would be straightforward: the more consequential an AI use becomes, the stronger the explanation, independent scrutiny and route to appeal should be.

For our school, that means asking who approved the tutor, what evidence supports its use, who can stop it and what happens when a student is harmed. For a powerful model developer, it means asking who can investigate its claims and what happens if its safeguards fail.

There is reason for hope in having several ways to exert influence: public institutions can set boundaries, researchers can test claims, communities can contribute knowledge and organisations can choose more accountable uses.

AI's benefits do not require handing one company, government or technical committee unquestioned authority. People should be able to understand who made an important decision, challenge it and see something change when the challenge is justified.
